list.listitem: Consider bladder pain syndrome (BPS) and interstitial cystitis (IC) in a patient with otherwise unexplained pelvic area pain, urinary frequency, and urgency. C
Confirm IC diagnosis with cystoscopy. C
There is no moderate- or high-certainty evidence establishing the efficacy of conservative, pharmacologic, and surgical treatments for BPS. Treatments are directed toward symptom relief. B

Oral therapy with pentosan polysulfate and amitriptyline, B and bladder installation therapy (with dimethyl sulfoxide [DMSO]) C are the cornerstone therapies for IC, in addition to pain control measures.
Hydrodistention and ulcer excision may provide short-term symptomatic relief; urinary diversion with or without cystectomy is a treatment of last resort for IC. C

background.definition: The International Continence Society reserves the diagnosis of IC for those patients with typical histologic and cystoscopic features. "Classic" IC is characterized by severe bladder inflammation, fibrosis, and ulcer formation (Hunner's ulcers). IC is within the larger and more clinically useful category of bladder pain syndrome (BPS), defined as "the complaint of suprapubic pain related to bladder filling, accompanied by other symptoms such as increased daytime and night-time frequency, in the absence of proven UTI or other obvious pathology."

list.listitem: Community-based medical record review: 0.01/1000 (Olmstead County, Minnesota).
Kaiser enrollees in Pacific Northwest: 0.2/1000 for women and 0.04 per 1000 for men.
Self-reported symptoms from National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (1988-1994) and National Health Interview Survey (1989): 5/1000 for the overall population and 8/1000 for women.
Physician diagnosis from the Nurses' Health Study (NHS): 0.5 to 0.6/1000 for women.
In a managed care population, the rate was 1.9/1000 for women and 0.4/1000 for men. The rate decreased to 0.9/1000 for women and 0.2/1000 for men with cystoscopic diagnosis.
Mean annual healthcare cost per patient in 2002 was approximately $4000/y greater in patients with IC.
Costs are borne during the most productive years of life (35-64 years).
Etiology is unknown.
Viral and bacterial infections are not associated with the disease.
Dysfunction of bladder urothelial cells occurs.
Dysfunction may relate to production of antiproliferative factor, which prevents normal growth of bladder lining cells.
Diminished glycosaminoglycan layer of bladder epithelial cells is also hypothesized.

Patients with classic disease will present with single or multiple patches of reddened (and/or ulcerated) bladder mucosa. Bullous swelling and pale reddening of the periulcer area are often evident along with petechial bleeding. Ulcers are termed Hunner's ulcers.
Mast cell infiltration is common in classic IC.
Nonulcerative disease patients have normal initial appearance of the bladder. Glomerulations with associated with petechial bleeding during and after distention are evident.
No characteristic biopsy findings are found in patients with nonulcerative disease.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: First-degree relative with IC or BPS

list.listitem: Consider BPS or IC in a patient with otherwise unexplained pelvic area pain associated with urinary frequency and urgency. C
Only 10% of IC patients present with "classic" features of ulceration. C
Pelvic pain and urgency/frequency (PUF) symptom scale scores greater than 14 () and abnormal potassium sensitivity tests (PSTs) suggest the presence of IC. C

Differential.Differential_Features: History, possibly hematuria, evidence of calculi on ultrasound or intravenous pyelography (IVP)
Presence of lesions at time of symptoms
Abnormal Pap smear, colposcopy, biopsy, or imaging
History of therapy or exposure to known bladder irritants or cyclophosphamide
History of exposure, positive PPD, culture
Inflammation of the outer portion of the vagina

list.listitem: The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases Consensus Criteria for the diagnosis of IC are shown in .
The typical patient is over 30 and presents with urinary frequency (10-15 times per day) and suprapubic pain that increases with bladder filling and decreases with voiding.
Pain may be mild as long as the patient can urinate at the onset of pain but can also be constant and severe.
Pain can also be urethral, vaginal, low abdominal, low back, vaginal, and inguinal; patients may report pain with intercourse.
Urination relieves pain in 82% of patients with classic disease and 69% of non-ulcer patients.
Hematuria is common in patients with IC.

No physical symptom or sign can differentiate ulcer disease from non-ulcer disease (ie, blood in urine, pain centered at right lower abdomen, standing relieves pain, sharp pain, weight change or eating disorder, irritable bowel syndrome, dull aching pain, dyspareunia, and relief with urination).
After initial history and labs (UA, urine culture, negative urine cytology), the initial diagnostic test for patients with suspected IC is cystoscopy.
A PST conducted during cystoscopy is suggested for individuals with early disease who may not have lesions detected on cystoscopy.

The PST is 80% sensitive and highly specific (<1% false-positive rate). A positive PST (patient reporting pain or urgency or both) confirms the presence of a bladder epithelial permeability defect, but a negative test does not rule out the diagnosis.
The PUF patient questionnaire can be used as a screening tool to identify IC ().
PUF scores of 10 or higher and 15 or higher predict positive PSTs 82% and 84% of the time, respectively (which strongly suggests IC).
Individuals with scores of less than 2 are unlikely to have a positive PST/IC.
If diagnosis is suspected based on history, exclude other potential diagnoses with UA, urine culture, and urine cytology.
Have patient keep a symptom diary and use PUF symptoms score ().
First-line treatments include amitriptyline and behavioral strategies (food and beverage elimination, delayed voiding, etc.).
Refer to urologist, who may treat empirically or perform PST and cystoscopy to confirm the diagnosis.

There is no moderate- or high-certainty evidence establishing the efficacy of conservative, pharmacologic, and surgical treatments for bladder pain syndrome (BPS). Treatments are directed toward symptom relief. B
Once diagnosis of interstitial cystitis (IC) is established, pentosan polysulfate (PPS) serves as baseline treatment, B followed by additional multimodal treatment as indicated. C
Amitriptyline use is safe and effective for treatment of pain, urgency, and frequency for patients with IC. B
Bladder instillation therapy with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) provides short-term symptomatic relief. C
Nonpharmacologic strategies of bladder training, diet change, counseling, and physical therapy may be helpful but have not been studied in clinical trials. C
Treatments are directed toward symptom relief. Cystoscopic findings should not influence choice of treatment.

Based on a Cochrane network meta-analysis, there is no moderate- or high-certainty evidence establishing the efficacy of conservative, pharmacologic, and surgical treatments for bladder pain syndrome (BPS). Treatments are directed toward symptom relief.

The only FDA-approved oral therapy for IC is pentosan polysulfate (PPS) given 100 mg orally three times a day on an empty stomach. Small but statistically significant improvements in pain, urgency, and frequency versus placebo are seen. Response rates of approximately 50% are not dose dependent.

The only FDA-approved intravesical therapy is dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), instilled weekly for 6 weeks in a mix of DMSO, lidocaine, corticosteroids, and heparin. A response rate of 87% to 98% is seen, but 48% of patients experience mild transitory urethral pain/irritation; relapse rates are 5% to 40%. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of intravesical treatments, including DMSO, resiniferatoxin, BCG, PPS, oxybutin, and urinary pH alkalinization.

Tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amtriptyline 12.5-150 mg/d improve pain intensity, urgency, and 24-hour urinary frequency, with approximately 50% reporting a good to excellent response. A randomized trial of 271 patients that compared escalating doses of amitriptyline with placebo found no overall, difference in symptoms, though a post hoc subgroup analysis suggested that persons who reached a dose of at least 50 mg/d reported a higher response rate.
Hydroxyzine, used in combination with PPS, shows nonsignificant trend of improvement versus PPS alone.
Narcotics may be required for pain control (long-acting plus immediate release for breakthrough pain).
Intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) treatment: low response rates (21%) are seen versus placebo (12%), plus large number of adverse events in the treatment arm.

Addition of SC heparin (a sulfated polysaccharide and mast cell inhibitor) to PPS therapy resulted in a favorable global response in 24% of patients and improvement in pain symptom score (especially in those patients with a minor response to PPS).
Intravesical hyaluronic acid and hyaluronic acid/chondroitin sulfate: a systematic review of 10 studies (n=390) suggested improvements in symptoms and quality of life with bladder instillation.
Gabapentin has been recommended, but clinical trial data are lacking.

Uncontrolled case series found subjective improvement in IC symptom scores with injection of botulinum toxin A in the bladder submucosa, with symptom improvements lasting an average of 3.7 months. Two systematic reviews of intravesical instillation of botulism toxin A found similar improvements.

A trial randomized 47 patients meeting clinical criteria for interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome were randomized to bladder instillations or intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA injections. At 2 months all patients improved but those receiving botulinum toxin injections improved more (O'Leary-Sant score 6.3 for botox vs 9.6 for installations, p = 0.008). However, this benefit did not persist at 6 to 9 months.
Hydrodistention is associated with short-term and sometimes dramatic improvement of symptoms in most patients.
Endoscopic cauterization or ablation of ulcers: 9/10 patients who had classic IC with Hunner's ulcers experienced symptom relief; some experienced lasting relief of up to 3 years.
Sacral nerve stimulation (InterStim): FDA approved for nonobstructive urinary retention, urinary urgency-frequency, and urge incontinence. Used for IC but clinical trials are lacking.
Urinary diversion with or without cystectomy is generally considered a treatment of last resort. Some patients continue to experience pelvic pain.
Calcium glycerophosphate (Prelief) and acupuncture have been recommended, but no clinical trials have been conducted.
Hyperbaric oxygen: response of 21% in 1 small study involving 30 treatment sessions.
Behavioral therapy should include dietary restrictions (avoidance of acidic foods or other irritants), bladder training to improve bladder capacity, and relaxation techniques.
Counseling as needed; treatment of depression, social isolation, anxiousness, and suicidal ideation as indicated.
Help patients to stop smoking.
The Interstitial Cystitis Association website (www.ichelp.org) offers dietary guidelines for IC sufferers.
Recommend avoidance of many fruits, juices, alcohol, carbonated beverages, coffee, tea, and a variety of common foods and condiments; however, good clinical trials are lacking.
Refer to a urologist for cystoscopy when the initial diagnostic and treatment measures suggest BPS or IC.
Hospitalization is rarely indicated; the condition is largely managed on an outpatient basis.
Referral to pain management specialist may be indicated.
Frequent follow-up and multimodal therapy are often required. C
Symptoms may plateau after 5 years. C
There is no evidence that therapy of mild disease prevents progression to more severe disease. C
There is no clear evidence that mild disease relentlessly progresses to more severe disease.
There is no evidence that therapy of mild disease prevents progression to more severe disease.
Patients may be symptomatic for as long as 7 years prior to correct diagnosis.
Decreased quality of life is common.
Younger patients (<40 years of age) typically have milder symptom and shorter duration and may respond to monotherapy.
Older patients (age >40) typically have more moderate to severe disease activity and may require a more multimodal approach.
A possible plateau in frequency and urgency symptoms occurs after approximately 5 years of symptoms.
Follow-up is tailored to symptom severity, duration, and response to therapy.
Use of scales such as the PUF Questionnaire is helpful for monitoring symptoms.
Regular follow-up visits are needed to assess and modify the treatment plan based upon response.
Although a clear cause and definite treatment for IC are lacking, ongoing research provides hope.
The diagnosis of IC is largely based on clinical symptoms after other possible conditions are evaluated.
Although cystoscopy (and sometimes biopsy) is often required, the procedure is brief and usually with low risk of complications.
Multimodal therapies are commonly used and may include medications, lifestyle changes, and surgery.
IC is most often seen in older adults.
However, there are no data from clinical trials specific to IC in older adults.
Symptomatic treatment is recommended.
Amitriptyline is pregnancy category C; caution advised in lactation.
Hydroxyzine is pregnancy category C; caution advised in lactation.
IC is exceptionally rare in children.

feature.caption: National Institute of Arthritis, Diabetes, and Digestive and Kidney Diseases Consensus Criteria for the Diagnosis of Interstitial Cystitis.
feature.feature_body:
Automatic Inclusion Hunner's Ulcer
Positive factors Pain on bladder filling relieved by emptying
Pain (suprapubic, pelvic, urethral, vaginal or perineal)
Glomerulations on endoscopy
Decreased compliance on cystometrogram
Exclusionary criteria <18 years old or duration <12 months
Bacterial, radiation, cyclophosphamide, or tuberculosis cystitis
Vaginitis
Symptomatic urethral diverticulum
Uterine, cervical, vaginal, or urethral cancer
Benign or malignant bladder tumors
Active herpes
Bladder or lower ureteral calculi
Waking frequency <5 times in 12 hours or nocturia <2 times
Symptoms relieved by antibiotics, urinary antiseptics, urinary analgesics
Involuntary bladder contractions (urodynamics)
Capacity >400 cc, absence of sensory urgency
Patient must have glomerulation (evident after hydrodistention under anesthesia with 80-100 cm of water pressure) or classic Hunner's ulcers on cystoscopic examination. Glomerulations must be diffuse, be present at a rate of 10 glomerulations per quadrant, and not be along the path of the cystoscope. From Gillenwater JY, Wein AJ. Summary of the National Institute of Arthritis, Diabetes, Digestive and Kidney Diseases Workshop on Interstitial Cystitis, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, Maryland, August 28-29, 1987. J Urol 1988;140:203-206.
